Gut

Is Leaky Gut Real? What the Research Actually Says

By Adam Seay, D.C., Root Health, Garner, NC. Updated October 2, 2026.

The short answer

Yes, in a narrower sense than the internet suggests. Increased intestinal permeability is a real, measurable state that mainstream gastroenterology researchers study.1 The commercial version, a zonulin test plus a supplement bundle, runs well ahead of the evidence, and the most widely used zonulin test does not measure what it claims to.2 Both of those statements are true at once.

What is real

Your gut lining has to let nutrients through and keep almost everything else out. The seals between the cells that line it, called tight junctions, open and close in response to food, microbes and inflammation. Zonulin is an established regulator of that opening, and the science behind it is solid.3

A 2019 review in the journal Gut lays out the parts of the barrier, the research methods that validly measure permeability, such as sugar probe tests using lactulose and mannitol, and the conditions in which barrier function measurably gets worse. The same review cautions that popular leaky gut claims need confirmation before anyone endorses elimination diets or repair supplements on the strength of them.1 I agree with both halves of that.

What is oversold

Zonulin the molecule and zonulin the lab test are in very different shape. An analysis of the most widely used commercial zonulin test found that it does not detect the molecule it is named for, and picks up other proteins instead.2 So a zonulin number on a commercial result, from blood or stool, is not a validated measurement. I do not treat any zonulin level as a diagnosis, and no practice should.

Skeptics overreach in the other direction. "Everyone's gut is permeable, so skip it" is right about the tests and wrong about the body. Of course the gut is permeable; you could not absorb food otherwise. That is like dismissing high blood pressure because everyone has blood pressure. The real question is whether the barrier has become too permeable.

What is known to stress the barrier

  • NSAIDs. Regular ibuprofen, naproxen or aspirin can damage the small bowel lining in ways capsule endoscopy can see and a standard scope cannot reach.4
  • Antibiotics. A course can shift the gut's bacterial makeup for months, and in one study the effects were still visible up to two years later.5
  • Psychological stress. In human studies, acute stress increased intestinal permeability through mast cells in the gut wall.6
  • Gluten, for some people. Celiac disease is the clear case. Non-celiac gluten sensitivity is a recognized category of its own, separate from celiac disease and wheat allergy.7

How I actually approach it

I read gut markers as pattern evidence alongside your symptoms, your history and how you respond over time. No single number, zonulin least of all, diagnoses a leaky gut by itself. In practice that means:

  • Test for celiac disease before cutting gluten, because the test only works while you are still eating it.
  • Remove the obvious stressors first. That includes talking with your doctor about regular NSAID use, rather than quitting a prescribed medication on your own.
  • Choose testing by your symptoms. Bloating, irregular bowels or a history of H. pylori point toward a comprehensive stool panel. Gut symptoms with food reactions point toward a wheat and gluten reactivity panel first. Brain fog alongside gut symptoms may add an organic acids test. Each of these is read as suggestive, not diagnostic.
  • Judge progress by how you feel over weeks and months, not by a single repeat test.

Common questions

Is there a reliable test for leaky gut?

Research labs use sugar probe tests such as lactulose and mannitol. Commercial zonulin tests are not reliable. Antibody panels against barrier proteins are suggestive pattern evidence, better than a bare zonulin number, and still not a stand-alone diagnosis.

Do I need to cut out gluten?

If you have celiac disease, yes, strictly. If not, test for celiac first while still eating gluten, then decide. A time-limited trial off gluten is reasonable if you judge it by how you feel.

Can stress really affect my gut?

Yes. Human studies show acute psychological stress increases intestinal permeability through mast cells in the gut wall.
